title_original: In Brussels, Photographers Set the Sun-Drawing Alight
excerpt_original: On the occasion of photography's bicentenary, France's Centre national des arts plastiques and Brussels' Hangar present "Reinventing Photography," an ambitious and electrifying exhibition: twenty Belgian and French artists interrogate, unsettle and resurrect the medium with…

blocks.text: Two hundred years ago, Nicéphore Niépce set a tin plate before his Burgundian window and waited. Hours passed; light did its work. No brush, no chisel — only the chemical reaction of Judean bitumen under the sun, and the world inscribed itself, unaided, onto a sensitive surface. His contemporaries called it the “sun-drawing,” with the same wonder that would seize, seventy years later, the audiences of the Lumière brothers watching their first cinematic projection: a train pulling into the station at La Ciotat.

In the age of artificial intelligence, images can still be born without a camera. The “this-has-been” so dear to the philosopher of the image Roland Barthes, that certainty that some real thing had once stood before a lens, no longer holds. In 2026, faces, landscapes and hyperrealistic scenes are conjured from nothing. It is within this great technological trembling that the Cnap and the Hangar — a Brussels art centre dedicated to contemporary photography — commissioned twenty artists: fifteen French, five Belgian, selected through an open call. Neither nostalgia nor ritual celebration, but a shared experiment in what the medium might yet become.

The return to origins begins with matter. Brussels-based artist Julie Calbert recovers the chemical residues of analogue photography, reintroduces them into the laboratory and sets them back in motion. From the photosensitive surface emerge phenomena of formation, propagation and erosion that she calls “unstable cartographies.” The image arrives on its own, with an almost organic autonomy: photography reclaims its original condition — a chemical reaction left to itself — and the artist reclaims hers, as a witness who guides without commanding.

Others surrender to time. French photographer Marie Bovo shoots at night, on a large-format camera, with exposures lasting up to nine hours, lit by nothing but the moon and the stars. Her “Forêts d’Hypnos” series stretch from the mimosa groves of the Tanneron to the hills of Tipaza, in Algeria, where vegetation has overgrown ancient Muslim graves from the colonial era. The night sky is streaked by the luminous trails of satellites while the trees hold centuries of buried memory, “immobile condensations of movements perceptible only through duration.”

More radical still: the renunciation of the gesture itself. In a valley of the Haute Maurienne, in the Alps, photographer and documentary filmmaker Michel Slomka scatters a constellation of camera traps and surrenders the shutter to the forest, the wind, the seasons, the passage of wolves. These devices, he notes, are “less surveillance cameras than small, motionless witnesses.” He has simply “tried to reduce the human footprint to a minimum” so that the animal’s footprint leaves, in the end, a photographic one. The work poses the question: who, exactly, makes the photograph?

It remained to make the dead speak. French artist Stéphanie Solinas unearthed eighteen portraits of young women from the nineteenth century on the American West Coast, driven by a single question: “What do you have to say to me today?” Drawing on a chain of tools running from mediumship to artificial intelligence, the installation “Une sorte de bordel” (2026), on the second floor of the Hangar, conjures from these pioneers a contemporary and animated lineage. A table called “diseuse” — fortune-teller — fitted with a tactile silicone hand, invites the visitor somewhere between oracle and dating app. Algorithms have replaced the ouija board.

On the floor below, the spectacular installation by visual artist François Bellabas rises like a monolith: a body-scale screen pours out an abstract, sonorous matter from which an embryo of his double surfaces, sharpens, dissolves, is reborn. The artist fed an algorithm on his own images, then “cut the process” at the moment when forms are still abstract, before the machine could complete its invention. “Our images, turned into fuel for machines, are computed in alien times”: by intercepting that stream, he grants his digital double “a space in which to take form.” The longer the visitor lingers, the more the double solidifies. It is the viewer who ends up being watched.

The same tension — between the photographer and his machinic double — inhabits the work of Sébastien Van Malleghem. A seasoned photojournalist with fifteen years of social documentary practice in black and white across northern Europe, he pivots with “V”(2026) toward colour, toward the light of Madeira and the Azores, and toward the machine. His prints on baryta paper hang in dialogue with a film generated entirely by AI from his own photographs. “Where photography offers a space of calm and beauty, its animated double provokes a diffuse unease,” he notes. A way of anchoring the living in paper, and holding anxiety at arm’s length.

Laurent Millet, meanwhile, seeks weight in the places where photography resists. “I nearly gave up photography several times because of its thinness, which I could find unbearable,” he confides. His theatres of illusion and scale models, built from nineteenth-century techniques now accessible to all, set a sculptural density against the medium’s transparency. The more objective an image becomes, he argues, the more it operates as a window that erases itself: he demands that it be “something very present, concrete, that pushes back against the eye.”

“To speak of the Bicentenary,” says Delphine Dumont, director of the Hangar, “is necessarily to interrogate the time in which we find ourselves.” The time of history, of creation, of institutions? Perhaps above all, she suggests, “the time proper to art: a time that escapes calendars, but leaves traces.” The poet Théophile Gautier wrote as much in 1864, in a phrase the exhibition catalogue exhumes as its epigraph: “The sun is tireless and photographers will not succeed in exhausting its patience.” Two hundred years after the Point de vue du Gras , other suns are rising over Brussels.
“Reinventing Photography” is on view at the Hangar, Brussels , until 20 December 2026.

The Hangar publishes 200 Years Later: Photography Reinvented by Five Belgian Artists , a leporello devoted to the five Belgian artists in the exhibition — Hangar Edition (2026) . The CNAP and Éditions Poursuite (Arles) co-publish Réinventer la photographie , a book bringing together invited texts and an essay by Jean-Christophe Bailly on the fifteen French artists exhibited (2026) .
